title: Choose a visualization for a question (preview)

blocks.content: Practice choosing a visualization from the viewer's question. Start with the question: a current value, proximity to a limit, comparison across categories, share of a total, or exact row values. Follow each question to a stat, gauge or bar gauge, bar chart, pie chart, or table.
Use the demo dashboards on Grafana Play. You don't need to create resources. Any editor changes are temporary. Leave without saving.
Explore the panels that show one value and how the stat visualization displays it.
Open **Sample Website Dashboard** in full-dashboard view.
Find the two panels that show one large number: **Support calls** and **Sign ups**. Each is a stat.
Open **Support calls** on its own.
Read the number. The panel title tells you what it counts. The faint line beneath it sketches how the value moved, but the number is what the viewer takes in at a glance.

Name the question this panel is built to answer: "What is the current number of support calls?" Compare it with **server requests** on the same dashboard, which answers how a value changed over time instead.
A stat suits a key metric you want to check at a glance. When the viewer needs the trend, a time series says more.
You've found the stats on a dashboard and read what each one tells you. Choose a stat when the question needs one value rather than a trend or a comparison.
Explore a gauge and a bar gauge to see how each one shows a value within a range and answers "How close is the value to a limit?"
Open the **Memory** gauge on **Grafana Dashboard**.
Find the displayed value and follow the filled arc around the gauge. The gauge adds position within a configured range that a value-only stat doesn't show.

Open the panel menu and select **Edit**. Under **Standard options**, read **Min** and **Max**: this example uses 0 and 300. Range endpoints don't have to appear as labels on the gauge, so inspect the settings rather than guessing the limit.
The range is a display setting. In this demo it isn't a real memory capacity, so check where a gauge's limit comes from before trusting it.
Leave the editor without saving and open the horizontal **Google hits** bar gauge.

Find a bar's number and follow its length across the available range. A bar gauge expresses position in a range with a bar instead of an arc. Don't confuse it with a bar chart that compares categories on a shared axis.
You've read a gauge and a bar gauge as values within configured ranges. Choose them when proximity to a limit matters, and check what the limit is.
Explore a bar chart to see how it answers "How do the values for different categories compare with each other?"
Open the **Popular JS Frameworks** bar chart.
Stars, forks, and watchers are three different GitHub counts for each library's repository.
Find **Vue** and **React.js**. Compare their green **Github Stars** bars, using the legend to keep the measure the same. Vue's bar is longer in this fixed sample.

The library names form categories; the star counts supply numeric values. Bar lengths on a shared scale answer "Which included library has more stars?" Stars, forks, and watchers measure different actions, not how many people use each library.
You've compared one numeric measure across categories. Next, read the same star counts as shares of a total.
Explore a pie chart to see how it answers "How much of the total does each part make up?" and what that total includes.
Open the **Popular JS Frameworks** pie chart.
Find **Vue** and **React.js** in the legend. Compare the sizes of their slices.

The larger slice represents a larger share of the included star counts. All six libraries' slices add to 100%. The whole is their combined count, not all libraries, all developers, or all library usage.

The bar chart answers "Which count is larger?" The pie answers "What share of this included total does each count represent?" Use a pie only when adding the numeric values produces a meaningful whole.
You've read a share and defined its denominator. Next, inspect the row-level detail that summary charts leave out.
Explore a table to see how it answers "What are the exact values, row by row?" and what it lets you do that a chart doesn't.
Open **Top 50 Post Data** on the **Visualizing Google Sheets Data** dashboard.
Each row is one forum post. The column headings, **id**, **title**, **reply_count**, **views**, **last_posted_at**, **category_id**, and **status**, tell you what each cell holds.
Find the post with the most **views**. Read its **title**, its **status**, and when it was last posted. The table gives you every field of that record at once.
Click the **reply_count** heading. The rows re-sort by that column, descending first and ascending on the next click. Which post has the most replies? Is it the same post that has the most views?

Pick two posts with the same **status** and compare their **views** exactly. A bar chart could show which bar is longer. Only the table gives you the two numbers, with the title, date, and category beside them.

Match the question to the display: one value uses a stat, position within a range uses a gauge or bar gauge, category comparison uses bars, share of a total uses a pie, and record-level detail uses a table.
You've matched six visualizations to the questions they answer: stat, gauge, bar gauge, bar chart, pie chart, and table. Continue with time series when the question asks how values change over time.
